title: Relevance
lines: Relevance asks what deserves attention when creating competent work becomes inexpensive.
It separates relevance from quality, novelty, popularity, and compliance with a brief.
The same artifact can matter differently as its audience, purpose, or circumstances change.
The book develops that argument across research, literature, film, design, and visual art.
Readers gain a framework for defending judgments while preserving space for unfamiliar work.

title: Keep the artifact, change the context
chapter: Keep the artifact, change the context
lines: A method can matter urgently to one community and remain peripheral to another.
Its technical properties need not change when the surrounding decision does.
The book therefore treats relevance as an argued relationship, rather than an intrinsic score.
Evidence about craft or novelty can inform that judgment without settling it.
This distinction connects its scientific examples with its discussion of culture and design.

title: Make the judgment inspectable
lines: A relevance dossier begins with the decision, affected people, values, constraints, and time horizon.
It connects specific claims to evidence, uncertainty, and possible counterarguments.
Different critics may assess feasibility, novelty, user value, or cultural contribution.
Their disagreement is useful information, not noise that a final score must erase.
The book also warns that multiple evaluators can share the same mistakes.

title: Leave room for the unfamiliar
lines: A system trained on earlier success can overlook work whose value is not yet recognized.
The book therefore preserves a role for exploration and difficult-to-classify contributions.
Its chapters ask how institutions can explain selection without fully optimizing inherited preferences.
Relevance is useful when competent output has become abundant and attention remains limited.
Read it to examine both the reasons for choosing work and the costs of overlooking it.
